extracted.intended_audience: historians, students, and general readers interested in the history of advertising and theatre print culture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and describes historical conventions, legal arrangements, and typical content/features of handbills, inscriptions, playbills, and show-advertisements from sixteenth–nineteenth-century England. Focuses on how such bills were produced, posted, and read (and on contemporary reactions to their style and morality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Playbill core content (time/place/nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Playbills customarily give information concerning the time, place, and nature of plays to be acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book states: 'it is shown to exist prior to the year 1563' and quotes John Northbrooke: 'They use to set up their bills upon posts some certain days before, to admonish people to make resort to their theatres.' Examples in the text show explicit listing of performance day/time, the theatre name, and the descriptive title of the piece (e.g., 'KING RICHARD THE THIRD').

rubrics_metrics.name: Playbill cast and character listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Playbills often list the parts/characters and the names of the actors performing them (though early playbills sometimes omitted these).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malone is cited: early playbills did not contain a list of characters or actors, but later bills commonly printed cast lists (see multi-line cast examples in 1741 and 1758 bills). Example bills in the chapter include full role-to-actor mappings and notes about performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre signaling on playbills (comedy/tragedy) and colour convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills indicate whether a piece is a comedy or a tragedy; tragedies were often printed in red ink for distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Shirley's 'Cardinal' prologue: the bill determines not the genre; the chapter says 'it may be inferred that the names of tragedies... were usually ... printed in red ink.' Hence a visual typographic convention (red for tragedy) is noted as a historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and posting practice for bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills were customarily affixed to posts and at stated or customary public places (posts, doors, gates, church doors, Guildhall, Blackwell Hall, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly notes bills 'were stuck upon posts' and cites Parliament's appointment of specific sites for affixing bills concerning sales: 'outer gate and upon the hall door of Sir Richard Gourney's house... north door of St Paul's Church... gate of Guildhall... gate of Blackwell Hall.' The derivation of 'poster' from 'posts' is also observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing and licensing/prerogatives for bills
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to print playbills was regulated: Stationers' Company and later royal patents granted privileges to particular printers for bills and related broadside material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter documents that the Stationers' Company conferred upon John Charlewood the privilege of sole printer of bills for players in 1587, earlier printed by James Roberts, and later a 1620 broadside shows James I granting patents for the sole printing 'of paper and parchment on the one side' explicitly covering 'Bills for Playes...'. This is a legal/procedural requirement for legitimate bill production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playbill format and complementary marketing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Playbills commonly include supplementary marketing and logistical elements: ticket prices, booking places, timing (e.g., 'Concert will begin at Six o'Clock'), lists of additional entertainments (dancing, ballad opera, pantomime), and occasionally notes on scenery/props.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show boxed ticket pricing (BOXES, PIT, GALLERY), instructions 'Places for the Boxes to be taken at...', notices that 'Between the two Parts will be presented...' and appended entertainments like 'A SPLENDID PANORAMA' or 'HARLEQUIN FAUSTUS!'. The bills also sometimes include N.B. notes about staging (flowers at altar), logistical accommodations (converting stable to boxes), and that performances may be 'for their Diversion' or 'Gratis'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show-bill spectacle and staging features as advertising content
rubrics_metrics.description: Show advertisements emphasize spectacle elements—scenery, illumination, music, costumes, panoramas, and novelty acts—to attract audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Richardson's Theatre description details extravagant external decoration, 'fifteen hundred variegated illumination-lamps', bands in scarlet, performers displayed on platform, and explicit hype for new melodrama and pantomime. Such material features are used as selling points on bills and handbills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, bilingualism, and patriotic/formal phrases in show bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Show adverts sometimes appear in multiple languages and employ formal or patriotic phrases (e.g., Latin 'Vivat Rex', French columns), and adapt language to appeal to varied audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showbill of William and Mary era prints English and French columns side-by-side and uses 'Vivat Rex' under the French, while an English equivalent 'God save the King' appears in the other column. The Italian opera bill (1811) uses Italian stage directions and formal licensing notice 'Com licenca.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of literary correctness and the critique of illiterate inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chapter critiques poorly written inscriptions and handbills, using them as examples of the ridicule and danger of advertising without rudimentary education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous window inscriptions and shop-bills are quoted verbatim showing bad spelling/grammar (e.g., 'Pryce Dyas... daler in Bacco Shag and Pig tail', 'Notice I dont keep twelve hole mousetrap nor penney ones...'), with the author commenting that such examples 'afford a vivid idea of the danger of venturing upon literature without the precaution of first learning the rudiments of education.' This functions as an implicit quality criterion: adverts should use correct and clear language to avoid ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms and self-regulation promised by theatrical practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: In defending theatres against prohibition, actors' remonstrance pledges behavioral and programmatic standards: prohibit unaccompanied females, restrict tobacco, expel ribaldry, and reform stage disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from 'The Actors' Remonstrance': promises include that 'no female whatsoever shall be admitted unless accompanied by her husband or some male relative', tobacco 'to be forbidden even in the threepenny galleries, except in the case of the pure Spanish leaf', and a general vow 'to expel all ribaldry from the stage' and 'amend all our amisses.' These are presented as moral and disciplinary standards actors offered to preserve their profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrimonial advertisement content expectations and social critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Matrimonial advertisements often list exhaustive personal specifications (appearance, languages, fortune, height) and instruct correspondents to send photograph and address to the editor; the author criticizes the public exposure and gullibility involved in such notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ad text includes detailed desirata ('talented, speaking or understanding French and Italian... in height about 5 feet 6 to 8 inches... must possess in her own right considerable fortune... Photograph and address with Editor'). The chapter comments this public exposure 'threatens to prolong this chapter unduly' and argues that a paternal government 'should fulfil its metier by preventing the public exposure of idiotcy,' framing a normative critique of such ads as potentially exploitative or ridiculous.
